title: Resultant of an equivariant polynomial system with respect to direct product of symmetric groups: the discriminant decomposition formula (Theorem 3.2)
author: Sonagnon Julien Owolabi; Ibrahim Nonkane; Joel Tossa
work: Resultant of an equivariant polynomial system with respect to direct product of symmetric groups
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the decomposition formula for the discriminant of a homogeneous polynomial invariant under the direct product of two symmetric groups, printed as Theorem 3.2 of the paper (native source0.tex lines 743--788), delivered together with the author's own complete proof of it (source0.tex lines 790--792, a proof environment closed by the author). The statement is one of the two main theorems of the paper: it is the theorem the paper's Example 3.3 immediately specialises to a degree-4 invariant polynomial to produce a factorised discriminant, and it is the four-regime refinement (p<d or p>=d, q<d or q>=d) of the paper's general decomposition formula for resultants, Theorem 2.1. The proof retained is genuinely complete as printed: it records that the four formulae are obtained from Theorem 2.1 by specialisation, and it identifies the single point where the specialisation is not formal, namely that the polynomials f^{i} being decomposed are the partial derivatives of an invariant homogeneous polynomial of degree d and therefore have degree d-1 and not degree d, which is exactly why the exponents mu_1, mu_2 and the lower bounds on the partitions r_1, r_2 change from the version in Theorem 2.1. Why this is beyond ordinary qualifying-examination material: the input to the specialisation is the paper's Theorem 2.1, whose proof the paper gives only as an idea and explicitly defers to an extended version, so the reader must reconstruct the resultant splitting by divided differences of an S_{1..p} x S_{p+1..n}-equivariant system; the discriminant side requires the classical identity d^{a(n,d)} Disc(f) = Res(f^{1},...,f^{n}) with a(n,d) = ((d-1)^n - (-1)^n)/d, the observation that the partial derivatives of an invariant polynomial form an equivariant system (the paper's Lemma 3.1, retained here with its complete proof), and then tracking, in four regimes, which partitions survive, on which side the exceptional factor f^{1,...,d+1} or f^{p+1,...,p+d} appears, and how the exponents mu_1 and mu_2 compensate it. Both the statement and the proof are the authors' own text line for line; nothing is re-derived. H2.
